title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali

attribution.tradition: Composed by Patañjali as a re-teaching (anuśāsana, 1.1) of the yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha (Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa on 1.1); Patañjali is regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the lord of serpents, and identified with the grammarian of the Mahābhāṣya.
attribution.scholarly: Most scholars doubt that the Yoga author is the grammarian (c. 2nd c. BCE). Philipp A. Maas argues, following earlier arguments by J. Bronkhorst, that sūtras and bhāṣya form one work — the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, as the colophons ('pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre') call it — by one author, c. 325–425 CE; others treat the sūtras as older than the bhāṣya.

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (Patañjali as an incarnation of Śeṣa)

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE together with the bhāṣya (Maas); earlier proposals range from the 2nd c. BCE to the 5th c. CE

structure.description: 4 pādas: Samādhi (51 sūtras), Sādhana (55), Vibhūti (55), Kaivalya (34) = 195 sūtras in the Vyāsa-based vulgate (Ānandāśrama ed., and every local commentary e-text). Some editions count 196 by treating 'etena śabdādy antardhānam uktam' — part of the bhāṣya on 3.21 in the Ānandāśrama ed. — as a separate sūtra 3.22, shifting the later numbers of pāda 3 by one. This unit uses the 195-sūtra numbering.

summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana. It defines yoga as the stilling of the activities of the mind (1.2); teaches practice and dispassion, devotion to Īśvara and Oṃ, the obstacles and their remedies, the samāpattis and the kinds of samādhi (pāda 1); kriyā-yoga, the five afflictions, karma, the seer and the seen, and the first five of the eight limbs (pāda 2); concentration, meditation, samādhi, saṃyama, the transformations of mind and the powers with their warnings (pāda 3); and the sources of powers, karma and latent tendencies, the reality of objects, the non-self-luminosity of mind, the cloud of dharma and kaivalya (pāda 4).

editions.name: Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47 (ed. K. Ś. Āgāśe, Pune 1904); GRETIL e-text
Ph. A. Maas, Samādhipāda: das erste Kapitel des Pātañjalayogaśāstra zum ersten Mal kritisch ediert (Aachen 2006)

notes: Correction to the task list: the vulgate count is 195 (51/55/55/34), not 196; see structure.

title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)

attribution.tradition: By Vyāsa, identified with Veda-Vyāsa and with Bādarāyaṇa (Vijñānabhikṣu, Yogavārttika intro. and 1.1; Nārāyaṇatīrtha, Sūtrārthabodhinī intro.).
attribution.scholarly: The author's identity is unknown; Maas (following Bronkhorst and others) holds that sūtra and bhāṣya are one work by Patañjali; older scholarship placed the bhāṣya well after the sūtras. The bhāṣya cites 'Patañjali' by name once (3.44), a point used in this debate.

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if one work with the sūtras (Maas); older estimates placed it later (6th–8th c.)

structure.description: running prose commentary on all 195 sūtras, headed by a maṅgala verse to the lord of serpents; each pāda closes 'iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre ... vyāsabhāṣye'

summary: The oldest and authoritative commentary. It defines yoga as samādhi and names the five levels of mind (1.1); analyzes the vṛttis, the kleśas and their states (with a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state), karma and its fruition; gives the fourfold scheme modelled on medicine (2.15) and the sevenfold final insight (2.27); lists seated postures (2.46); explains saṃyama and the powers, the four kinds of yogin and the invitation of the celestials (3.51), and a detailed cosmology (3.26); and argues against Buddhist views of a momentary mind and of objects as mind-only (1.32, 4.14–24).

editions.name: Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47 (ed. K. Ś. Āgāśe, Pune 1904); GRETIL e-text
Pātañjaladarśana with Vyāsa's bhāṣya and Vijñānabhikṣu's Yogavārttika, ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (Calcutta); e-Bhāratī Sampat e-text

title: Tattvavaiśāradī

scholarly.text: 9th or 10th c. CE (Vācaspati's Nyāyasūcīnibandha is dated 898 of an era read as Vikrama = 841 CE or Śaka = 976 CE)

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's sub-commentary on Vyāsa's bhāṣya, the standard explanation of it. It answers the objection that Hiraṇyagarbha, not Patañjali, is the teacher of yoga by reading 'anuśāsana' as re-teaching (1.1), develops the theistic arguments of 1.24–26, and explains the objects of the samprajñāta samādhis in terms of the grasped, the grasping and the grasper.
notes: Content summarized from memory; only the TV on 4.1 is in the local DCS corpus.

title: Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti)

scholarly.text: first half of the 11th c. CE (reign of Bhoja of Dhārā, c. 1010–1055)

summary: King Bhoja's concise vṛtti on the sūtras (not on the bhāṣya). It sets out the four samprajñāta samādhis as savitarka, savicāra, sānanda and sāsmita, calls those who rest content in bliss 'videhas' and those who rest in I-am-ness 'prakṛtilayas', and treats discernment of the supreme puruṣa as the grasper-coalescence (1.17); asamprajñāta is reached by rejecting every arising activity 'not this, not this' (1.18); devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to the supreme teacher without desire for fruit (1.23, 2.1).

title: Yogavārttika

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's extensive sub-commentary on the bhāṣya. It calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda spoken by Vedavyāsa' and holds Sāṃkhya and the other darśanas to be contained in it like rivers in the ocean (intro.); cites the Yoga-Yājñavalkya for Hiraṇyagarbha as first teacher (1.1); argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi against a single-reflection view (1.7); gives its own account of the four samprajñāta samādhis (1.17); and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (1.51).

editions.name: ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (Calcutta), with the bhāṣya; e-Bhāratī Sampat e-text

title: Yogasārasaṅgraha

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's digest of the doctrine of the Yoga Sūtras as he expounds it in the Yogavārttika.
notes: Structure and contents not recalled in detail (gap).

title: Pātañjalayogaśāstravivaraṇa (Yogasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇa)

attribution.tradition: Colophons ascribe it to Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, pupil of Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
attribution.scholarly: Disputed. P. Hacker and T. Leggett argued that it is an early work of the Advaita teacher Śaṅkara; T. S. Rukmani and others doubt the ascription and date it later; K. Harimoto critically edited the section on YS 1.23–28.

scholarly.text: uncertain: c. 8th c. CE if by Śaṅkara; later dates proposed

summary: A sub-commentary on Vyāsa's bhāṣya, first printed in 1952 (Madras Government Oriental Series), notable for its extended reasoning about Īśvara (1.23–28) and for the controversy over its ascription to Śaṅkara.

title: Yogasūtravṛtti of Nāgeśa (Nāgojī) Bhaṭṭa
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras by the grammarian Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa. On 1.1 it says the śāstra expounds in detail the yoga taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and others; on 1.2 it glosses citta as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and nirodha as a special, supersensible effort that dissolves the activities.
notes: Nāgeśa is reported to have written a longer and a shorter vṛtti (Bṛhatī, Laghvī) — which one the local raw_etexts file contains is not verified.

title: Yogamaṇiprabhā

attribution.tradition: Colophon: by Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, paramahaṃsa pupil of Govindānanda; each pāda is called part of the 'sāṅkhyapravacana' and of the Yogamaṇiprabhā.

scholarly.text: late 16th – 17th c. CE (inferred from his teacher Govindānanda)

summary: A vṛtti that follows the bhāṣya (bhāṣyānugā). On 1.1 it explains 'anuśāsana': although the śāstra was made by Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, considering it extensive, begins a śāstra that follows it.

title: Padacandrikā of Anantadeva
summary: A short word-by-word commentary on the sūtras by Anantadeva, who says he made this Padacandrikā after examining 'the vṛtti on the meaning of the sūtras' and offers it at the feet of Śiva (closing verse); it glosses nirodha as the mind's inward dissolution into its cause (1.2).

title: Yogasudhākara
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras ('the speech of the lord of serpents') by Sadāśiva Brahmendra, composed, as its closing verses say, by the grace of the teacher and offered at the teacher's feet.

title: Yogasiddhāntacandrikā
summary: Nārāyaṇatīrtha's extensive vṛtti. Its opening verses give the transmission (Pitāmaha taught yoga; Śeṣa in the sūtras; Vyāsa in the bhāṣya; Vācaspati Miśra and Vijñānabhikṣu clarified the bhāṣya) and argue that Vyāsa's Brahma Sūtras refuted pradhāna's independence, not yoga as meditative cultivation; the introduction treats deep contemplation (nididhyāsana) as samādhi, 'also called rājayoga', and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.

title: Sūtrārthabodhinī
summary: A brief commentary by Nārāyaṇatīrtha, written at Prayāga (closing verse). Its introduction: liberation is the highest human aim, reached through hearing, reflection and deep contemplation; Patañjali composed the sūtras in four pādas; Bādarāyaṇa (Vyāsa) wrote the bhāṣya.

title: Yogasūtradīpikā (Pradīpikā) of Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: A commentary 'for the easy understanding of the slow-witted' by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, who says it condenses the meaning examined in the bhāṣya and 'by my teacher himself in the Vārttika' (Vijñānabhikṣu).

title: Bhāsvatī
summary: Hariharānanda Āraṇya's Sanskrit sub-commentary on the Yoga-bhāṣya, printed with the bhāṣya and other commentaries in the Kashi Sanskrit Series edition of the Yoga darśana (1935).

title: Pātañjalarahasya
summary: A gloss on Vācaspati Miśra's Tattvavaiśāradī by Rāghavānanda Sarasvatī, printed in the Kashi Sanskrit Series edition of the Yoga darśana (1935).

title: Yogavallī
summary: A modern Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Sūtras. Its introduction surveys the darśanas, gives the count of 195 sūtras (51, 55, 55, 34), notes that some manuscripts mark the end of the work after pāda 3, cites the verse from Bhoja's vṛtti on Patañjali's three kinds of purification, and compares the Vivaraṇa, Tattvavaiśāradī and Yogavārttika on particular sūtras.
notes: Only the Samādhipāda is in the local raw_etexts file; author and date not identified (gap).

title: Kitāb Pātanǧal (al-Bīrūnī's Arabic Patañjali)
alt_titles: Kitāb Bātanǧal al-Hindī fī al-ḫalāṣ min al-irtibāk (The Book of Patañjali the Indian on Liberation from Bondage)

scholarly.text: c. 1017–1030 CE (made in India; used in al-Bīrūnī's India, completed c. 1030)

summary: An Arabic rendering, recast as questions and answers, of a Pātañjala yoga text together with a commentary that is not Vyāsa's; known from a single manuscript in Istanbul, edited by H. Ritter (1956). An early witness to the Yoga Sūtra's reception outside India.
notes: Arabic title and manuscript details recalled, not checked.

title: Dharma Pātañjala

scholarly.text: surviving manuscript of the 15th c. CE (reported as 1467 CE); composition earlier

summary: An Old Javanese Śaiva text in dialogue form that presents a Pātañjala-type yoga within a Śaiva frame; edited and studied by Andrea Acri. Evidence for the transmission of Pātañjala yoga to Java.
notes: Recalled, not checked (manuscript date and details).
